transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Ortega (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Nexus EM), Priya Singh (Nexus ML), Liam O'Connor (Nexus Platform)

Summary:
Quick weekly sync for the POC focused on caching (prefix + KV), review of hit rates, tuning knobs, and next steps for increasing reuse / reducing per-token cost. Decent progress; still seeing lower prefix reuse for certain prompt families. Agreed actions to prototype prompt canonicalization and run stratified benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- Measured prefix cache hit rates by user flow
- KV cache behavior and eviction patterns
- Prompt reuse / normalization strategies (canonicalization, template IDs, TTL)
- Tradeoffs: cache granularity vs staleness, TTLs, warmers, and cold-start penalties
- Security & data retention/questions about logs
- Next steps and responsibilities

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining - quick check-in, we have about 45 minutes. Samir, want to kick off with the hit-rate summary?
[00:20] Samir (SE): Yeah, sure. I sent the spreadsheet this morning - quick highlights: overall KV cache hit is around 84% for repeat session token lookups when the exact prompt key matches, but prefix cache hit is lower - about 62% overall. For the recommendations flow it drops to ~18% because prompts vary a lot.
[00:45] Maya (Nexus): When you say prefix cache is 62, is that after canonicalization or raw prompt text?
[00:55] Samir: Raw prompt text. We haven't applied the canonicalization rules yet for that run. So you can see the delta when we ran the small sample last week, canonicalization bumped similar flows by ~12-15 points.
[01:15] Priya: OK that matches what we suspected. Our users have a lot of dynamic fields - SKUs, location strings - so identical intents don't map to identical prefixes.
[01:30] Liam: Can you explain how you're hashing keys? We were debugging an apparent mismatch where similar prompts ended up in different keys.
[01:40] Samir: Sure - current prod-ish key is hash(model, route, prompt_text_trimmed_to_512). We also slugify whitespace and remove email-esque tokens in the preprocess. But it doesn't normalize synonyms or reorder clauses. So e.g., "Find red shoes size 9" vs "size 9 red shoes" are different.
[02:05] Maya: Right, that's the problem. We need semantic-level reuse, not just text-level.
[02:15] Samir: We're proposing a two-step approach: 1) lightweight canonicalization rules (normalize numbers, strip variable tokens, canonicalize order for known templates) and 2) attach a template_id to the request so the runtime can do prefix-key grouping at the cache layer. Simple prototype of 1) gave that +12-15% uplift in prefix hit for the catalog search family.
[03:00] Priya: Nice. Any downside - like correctness or hallucination risk when we canonicalize?
[03:10] Samir: Good question. The canonicalization is conservative - we only normalize parts we know are non-semantic (IDs, timestamps, user names). For intent-changing parts we leave them. We discussed adding a confidence tag so we can fall back to full run if mismatch occurs.
[03:30] Jamie: Also think about TTLs. Samir, what TTLs are we seeing that give best cost/latency tradeoff?
[03:40] Samir: For KV cache we have a 24h default and that's fine; for prefix cache we've been testing 30m, 1h, and 6h. 1h seems sweet spot for your traffic - gives good reuse during shopping sessions but reduces staleness. But for price/availability pages we saw 6h beneficial. We can set rules per route.
[04:10] Liam: How does the cache eviction interplay with dedicated vs hosted? If we move to dedicated pilot, will the hit rates improve just because of locality?
[04:25] Samir: Yes, dedicated pools reduce cross-tenant eviction pressure, so you'll see higher effective hit rates for cold-start sensitive flows. Also routing affinity keeps users on same pool. But dedicated has higher cost, so we'll measure cost/throughput tradeoffs in the pilot.
[04:45] Maya: Do we have numbers for cold starts? Like latency impact when a prefix miss goes to model?
[04:55] Samir: From the bench runs: cold token-generation latency increases 120-6300ms per request, depends on model size and batch. For your baseline 13B-ish model, median extra latency was ~180ms on a miss. If we warm prefixes or use short lived warmers the impact drops to ~50-680ms.
[05:20] Priya: Can we do an async background warmer for high-frequency templates?
[05:28] Samir: Absolutely - we can add a warmer job: when a route sees X unique requests per minute, spin a background warm call to refresh the prefix cache. It's basically pre-population. We discussed politeness and cost, but for heavy trafficked templates it's cheap.
[05:45] Liam: Any impact on cost accounting? We want token-level billing to reflect warmed requests vs cold runs.
[05:55] Jamie: We can tag warmed requests in logs and surface them on the Console - per-route CPU/token breakdown. We'll add that to next week's dashboard.
[06:10] Maya: Security question: where do cache keys live? Are keys or cached content written to logs?
[06:20] Samir: Keys are hashed and we do not persist raw prompt text in the cache store. Audit logs can be configured - by default Redwood doesn't persist PII; we support customer-managed key encryption and KMS integration for the cache backend. We'll send the SOC2 appendix.
[06:40] Maya: Cool. Please send us the security appendix.
[06:45] Jamie: Noted (Jamie -> send SOC2 appendix).
[06:50] Priya: Let's go back to the hit-rate breakdown by flow. Samir, can you run through the spreadsheet numbers?
[07:00] Samir: Sure. I split by route: search/catalog (45% of traffic): prefix hit 58% raw, KV 86%. Recommendations (20%): prefix hit 18% raw, KV 74%. Checkout assistance (10%): prefix 71%, KV 92%. Chat support bot (25%): prefix 39%, KV 80%. After applying canonicalization heuristics in the small test subset, search improved to 72% prefix, recs to 41%, overall weighted prefix hit moved from 62% to ~69%.
[08:00] Maya: That recs number is big - from 18 to 41 - that's promising. What heuristics did you apply for recs?
[08:10] Samir: For recs we removed session-scoped IDs and normalized filters order, and we replaced product lists with a product-list-hash token so different ordering doesn't change the key.
[08:30] Priya: That product-list-hash - is it deterministic across clients? Concern about client-side reordering causing misses.
[08:38] Samir: We compute canonical hash server-side after sorting the list; clients send the list, we canonicalize. We can also move canonicalization into the client lib to reduce server CPU but for now server-side is easier.
[08:55] Liam: CPU cost for canonicalization - do you have numbers?
[09:00] Samir: It's small: about 0.8ms per request on average for simple rules, up to 3-64ms for complex list hashing. For your QPS it's acceptable but we'll quantify in the staging run.
[09:15] Maya: On the product side, we think canonicalization is acceptable if we get that hit-rate bump - helps latency and cost.
[09:25] Jamie: Good. Any blockers on implementing canonicalization in staging?
[09:30] Priya: We'll need the ruleset and a library, plus tests. We can prototype a small Python/Node normalizer.
[09:40] Samir: We have an internal canonicalization repo and small example lib. I'll share it.
[09:45] Jamie: Action: Samir share lib + example rules.
[10:00] Maya: About measuring improvement - can we get stratified analytics? i.e., show hit-rate by user cohort and route?
[10:10] Samir: Yes, the spreadsheet has cohort slices. We'll instrument the next run to export by cohort: anonymous vs logged-in, mobile vs web, and 95th percentile session length.
[10:25] Priya: One more question - in some cases we saw slight quality regressions when we used aggressive templateing; examples where models mis-resolved ambiguous pronouns. Did you notice that?
[10:36] Samir: We saw rare regressions - about 0.3% of responses changed in a way the product team flagged. That's why we want a conservative rollout: shadow canonicalization, then a canary that allows fallbacks when the quality signal drops. We can wire your eval set to automatically rollback the rule if your QA threshold exceeds X.
[11:00] Jamie: Good safety net. Also we'll run A/B tests for customer-visible flows.
[11:08] Maya: What's the uplift we should expect for cost? Any back-of-envelope?
[11:12] Samir: For the canonicalization + 1h TTL + warmers on top templates, we estimate 18-24% reduction in token spend for the POC traffic mix. If you go dedicated and get higher effective cache locality, another 8-12% possible.
[11:30] Liam: Sounds compelling. We need to validate with pilot.
[11:35] Priya: On instrumentation, we also want precise attribution for warmed vs live tokens so our finance team can account.
[11:42] Jamie: We'll ensure request tags are emitted and visible in the Console; Samir will add warmed/request-tagging events.
[11:50] Samir: Noted. I'll add warmed flags and a "canonicalization_version" tag to logs so you can filter.
[12:00] Maya: Anything about persistence of cached responses and GDPR-data-residency? Some EU customers ask to avoid storing content longer than 30 days.
[12:10] Samir: You can set per-customer retention policies; the cache backend supports TTL and purge APIs. For EU data residency we can run caches in EU region under Private or Dedicated deployments. We'll add that detail to the security doc.
[12:30] Jamie: Quick recap of decisions: prototype canonicalization in staging, run stratified bench, add warmers for top N templates, instrument warmed flags and canonicalization version, share security/SOC2 doc, and schedule dedicated pilot for early May.
[12:55] Maya: Agreed.
[13:00] Priya: Ok next question - what about batching configuration? We saw some batching tradeoffs last week.
[13:10] Samir: Batching reduces per-token cost but increases latency variance. For the cached prefixes we can use smaller batch windows since cached responses are faster; it'll help throughput. We'll tune batch size and max wait per route. Our autoscaler can keep tail latency within SLO while batching.
[13:40] Liam: Anything else on the tuning front?
[13:45] Samir: TTL per route, template IDs for grouping, warmers for top templates, and optionally dedicated pools for high-throughput flows. Also we recommend a cache-heatmap dashboard - we can add that to Console next week.
[14:05] Maya: Great - can you share the heatmap mockup?
[14:10] Samir: I'll attach the mock to the spreadsheet.
[14:20] Jamie: Any blockers from Nexus side to start the staging canonicalization?
[14:25] Priya: We'll need the rules and the example lib. Also we want a list of top 100 templates to prioritize.
[14:35] Samir: We'll export top templates and share by EOD tomorrow.
[14:40] Jamie: Action items recap: Samir export templates + share lib; Priya run tests; Liam provision nodes; Jamie send security + pricing.
[14:55] Maya: Also send the spreadsheet with before/after canonicalization and the methodology note so our analytics team can reproduce.
[15:05] Samir: Will do. Link to shared sheet: https://redwood.internal/sheets/nexus-caching-results (note: placeholder)
[15:15] Priya: One last nit - in the logs we saw the term "KV cache" occasionally transcribed as "K-V cash" in the meeting notes; ignore that.
[15:22] Samir: Ha, noted. The auto-transcript sometimes mangles tech words.
[15:25] Jamie: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and set the pilot schedule.
[15:30] Maya: Thanks all.

Meeting end.
